title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ellington Township enacts a moratorium on new data centers while Genesee County gets its impact study.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're digging into Ellington Township's new moratorium on data centers and what it signals for communities across the state.
That's the big one this morning. Graham, walk us through what happened in Ellington.
Residents there pushed the board to approve a pause on any new data center proposals. It gives everyone time to look hard at power demands, water use, and how these projects might affect local taxes.
Why now? What sparked the push for the moratorium?
Folks in Ellington saw proposals coming in and wanted breathing room. The board listened and hit the brakes so they can study the real impacts before anything moves forward.
And Tuscola County neighbors are watching closely, right?
Exactly. Other townships in the area are paying attention to see how this plays out and whether similar pauses make sense for them.
Let's zoom out. Why are data centers such a flashpoint right now? What's the history here?
Michigan has seen a wave of interest in these facilities because of available land, fiber, and power infrastructure. But as proposals multiply, towns are realizing the scale of what they bring.
Scale meaning what exactly for everyday residents?
We're talking huge electricity loads that can strain the grid, big water needs for cooling, and questions about whether prime farmland gets converted. Local tax deals also come into play.
And how does that connect to electric bills? We've heard about DTE's rate request.
Data center demand is one reason DTE is asking for a big hike. Attorney General Nessel is pushing back hard on that, saying the full amount would hurt households too much.
So even if a town says no to a project, the power demand elsewhere can still show up on everyone's bill?
That's the ripple effect people are worried about. One big facility can influence rates across the region.
What about water? Is that as big an issue as power?
Cooling systems need a lot of it, especially in warmer months. Towns are asking how that affects aquifers and local supplies when multiple projects stack up.
And farmland? Are these going on ag land mostly?
Many proposals target open or agricultural areas because they're cheaper and have fewer neighbors. That raises questions about long-term land use and food production.
Who are the main players pushing back versus pushing forward?
Residents and some local officials want more study and rules. Developers and some economic development folks see jobs and tax revenue. It's a classic tension between growth and local control.
We've seen other townships pause too. How common is this becoming?
Solon Township just extended its freeze another six months. A couple of Metro Detroit suburbs rewrote zoning rules this week. It's spreading as more communities get proposals.
What happens next in Ellington specifically?
The moratorium buys time for the board to update rules and gather more data on impacts. Nearby towns will likely follow the outcome closely.
And statewide, new bills just dropped to regulate these projects. How do those fit in?
Lawmakers introduced measures aimed at power use, noise, and tax deals. They respond directly to the community pushback we've been seeing.
Will those bills slow things down or just add oversight?
Hard to say yet. They could give towns more tools without stopping projects outright.
Meanwhile Genesee County just got its own impact study delivered. What's in that?
A local panel finished its report on power, water, and road strain. Officials now have numbers to weigh against any future proposals.
Residents thirty miles away might want the same thing, right?
Absolutely. The study could become a model for other counties facing similar decisions.
Shifting to Saline, that project is still moving despite new rules. What's the latest there?
The proposal is advancing even as township officials tighten zoning under pressure. It could mean construction jobs but also heavy utility demands.
And those demands could affect rates for people farther away?
That's the concern. Power and water needs don't stop at township lines.
DTE is also talking about two new gas plants to meet this demand. What's the timeline on that?
They plan to ask regulators soon. Older coal plants are retiring, so these would help fill the gap but could mean more fossil fuel generation and higher bills if approved.
How are residents reacting to the idea of new gas plants?
Some see it as necessary for reliability. Others worry about the cost and emissions, especially with data centers driving the need.
Wixom got sued by a developer after blocking a project. What's at stake in that case?
The developer claims the zoning changes unfairly killed their plans. Taxpayers could end up covering legal costs, and the outcome might influence how other cities handle similar fights.
A recall effort failed against officials who approved a big project. What does that mean for opponents?
The clerk rejected the petitions, so the 500-acre facility stays on track. Opponents now have fewer options to revisit the rezoning vote.
Two more Metro Detroit towns changed their rules this week too. Any common thread?
Noise, water, and power concerns are driving the zoning updates. It's the same pattern repeating across the region.
For listeners, what should they watch this weekend?
No big public meetings on the calendar, but keep an eye on Tuscola County boards and any follow-up from the Genesee study. Things are moving fast at the local level.
And the bigger picture?
Communities are learning they have tools to slow down or shape these projects. The question is how those tools get used as demand keeps growing.
We'll be tracking it all. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow. Thanks for listening.

episode_title: Ellington Township Pauses Data Centers as Power and Water Scrutiny Grows
